summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta carries its own layer of discriminatory regional regulation. A 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people examined eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation. The regulations it documents include dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The mapping states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the eight it examined, so the categories it identifies are not confined to the provinces it names.

The most fully documented enforcement action against a trans institution in Yogyakarta is the February 2016 closure of Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women study Islam. The hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal the school, and on the night of 24 February 2016 a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta ended with an agreement to shut it. Those present included ward and residents' officials, the lurah and the local military district commander; an earlier session on 19 February was attended by the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. The district head justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site. Its founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction.

A waria witness at the meeting said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of "Allahu Akbar" and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, called LGBT people "sama-sama anak bangsa" (fellow children of the nation) and said the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds; no provincial anti-trans statute was cited.

The pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community were operating again years after the closure, and economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.
tangentialFactors: Enforcement against trans people in Yogyakarta has run through administrative and community pressure rather than an enacted provincial anti-trans statute. The 2016 closure followed a demand from a hardline group and was formalised by local officials on permit and religious grounds. The regional regulations documented for Yogyakarta and comparable provinces regulate public conduct and appearance, such as dress, curfews and where transgender people may appear, rather than criminalising same-sex activity.
localsOnly: Yogyakarta's trans women, known locally as waria or transpuan, are attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, and most work as street performers or wedding make-up artists. During the COVID-19 pandemic their earnings fell by about 60 percent; the community was ignored by the government and struggled to pay rent and buy food. On 12 June 2021 the pesantren hosted an aromatherapy-candle making class run with the local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills. The waria kept performing even as donors refused masked performances.
outOfScopeNotes: The 2022 mapping reports the categories of discriminatory regional regulation across its eight focus provinces and asserts that its findings extend further; it does not itemise which specific regulations apply in Yogyakarta. No enacted provincial anti-trans statute is cited in connection with the 2016 closure, which proceeded on administrative and community grounds. The inventory contains no documentation of the Yogyakarta pesantren's or the local trans community's position after 2021.
